newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Balladur sees left dropping vows for EMU.
newsitem.headline: France's Balladur sees left dropping vows for EMU.

text.p: Conservative ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur predicted on Wednesday that France's new leftist government would soon renounce its campaign vows on expensive social programmes in order to qualify for the euro.

He predicted that Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin would use an audit of public finances, expected to be completed later this month, as an excuse to ignore campaign promises that would require new spending and thus drive up public deficits, preventing France from honouring its European commitments.
"If France does not adhere to the single European currency, it will be humiliated and marginalised," Balladur said in an interview on French television TF1.

Jospin ordered the audit of public finances shortly after taking power early last month, saying he needed to know more about the true magnitude of public deficits run up by the previous conservative government before he could make decisions on key aspects of his economic programme.
Balladur said the audit would turn out to have been "a political operation, pure and simple, with no significant meaning, because we already know about the deficits."

He charged that Jospin had already gone back on campaign promises on the threatened closing of a Renault car assemby plant in Vilvoorde, Belgium, on privatisation policy and on a European Stability Pact.

Jospin found himself in the hot seat over another campaign promise on Wednesday after government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said the cabinet was weighing a possible tax increase on profitable companies to help bring down public deficits while funding new spending measures.
Trautmann's statement knocked French stocks, with the CAC-40 blue-chip index falling by more than two percent after rising earlier in the day.
Jospin during the campaign had ruled out new budget austerity to help France qualify for European economic and monetary union.
Tax increases were under study because the government hopes to limit the deficit to around 3.3 percent of gross domestic product this year to prepare France for EMU.
A government source has said the deficit could otherwise be more than 3.4 or 3.5 percent of GDP this year -- above a level seen as acceptable for EMU entry to France's EU partners.
